title: Phase 9: Observability with logs, metrics and traces
description: Project: Phase 9: Observability with logs, metrics and traces. Build and understand this project with step-by-step guidance.

data.text: You have built an expense platform with authentication, an API, background jobs, and caching. Now imagine it is running in production and a user reports that expense submissions are intermittently failing. Without logs, metrics, and traces, diagnosing the issue is a guessing game. Observability gives you the data to move from 'it is slow' to 'the database connection pool saturated at 2 PM during the reimbursement batch job.'

Observability is often confused with monitoring. Monitoring tells you when something is wrong based on predefined checks. Observability lets you ask arbitrary questions about the system's internal state from external outputs. A truly observable system lets you understand never-before-seen failure modes without shipping new code.

data.title: Three pillars of observability
items: Logs: timestamped records of discrete events, ideal for auditing and debugging specific requests
Metrics: numeric measurements over time, ideal for alerting and trend analysis
Traces: end-to-end records of requests across service boundaries, ideal for understanding latency and dependencies
Structured logging: emit logs as JSON with consistent fields so they are searchable and filterable
Golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, and saturation—the four metrics every service should expose
Service Level Indicator: a quantitative measure of service health, such as request latency or error rate
Service Level Objective: a target value for an SLI over a rolling window, such as 99.9% availability
Alert fatigue: the degradation of response quality when alerts are too numerous or too noisy

terms.definition: A method to track requests as they flow through multiple services by assigning a unique trace ID and recording spans for each operation.
A single unit of work within a trace, representing one operation such as a database query or an HTTP call.
An open-source observability framework that provides vendor-neutral APIs and SDKs for traces, metrics, and logs.
Logging in a consistent, parseable format such as JSON rather than free-form text, enabling powerful filtering and aggregation.
Four key metrics for monitoring distributed systems: latency, traffic, errors, and saturation.
The decreased response to alerts caused by receiving too many low-priority notifications, leading engineers to miss critical issues.

data.text: Most production debugging starts with logs. The difference between a painful investigation and a quick root-cause analysis is structured logging. Instead of 'User 123 submitted expense 456,' emit JSON with userId, expenseId, amount, category, and duration. That structure lets you filter, group, and aggregate without regex.

data.text: Metrics answer 'how is the system performing?' without requiring you to read individual log lines. Instrument the expense platform with counters for requests, gauges for queue depth and connection pool usage, and histograms for request latency. Export these to Prometheus or another metrics backend and build dashboards in Grafana.

data.title: Essential metrics for the expense platform
items: expense_api_requests_total: counter partitioned by route and status code
expense_api_request_duration_seconds: histogram for p50, p95, and p99 latency
expense_queue_depth: gauge showing the number of pending background jobs
expense_db_connection_pool_available: gauge for available database connections
expense_cache_hit_ratio: gauge showing Redis cache effectiveness

data.title: Avoid metric overload
data.text: Instrumenting everything sounds safe, but hundreds of metrics create dashboards nobody reads and alerts nobody trusts. Start with the golden signals for each service, then add domain-specific metrics only when you have a question they answer.

When a request crosses from the React frontend to the ASP.NET Core API, into the background job processor, and out to a payment provider, a single log line is not enough. Distributed tracing links every hop into a trace, showing you where time is spent and where failures occur.

cards.title: Self-hosted

data.text: Observability is not free. Storing every trace, metric, and log line indefinitely can cost more than the application itself. Use sampling for high-traffic services, set retention policies based on compliance needs, and archive cold data to object storage. A senior engineer treats observability costs as a first-class budget item.

data.title: Observability cost controls
items: Sample traces at 1-5% in production; use head-based sampling for consistency
Aggregate metrics at the source instead of sending raw metric streams
Set log retention to 7-30 days for debug logs and 90-365 days for audit logs
Use structured logging to avoid storing duplicate context in every log line
Archive old traces to S3 or Blob Storage for compliance instead of keeping them hot

items.question: How do I choose between logs, metrics, and traces?
items.answer: Use all three. Metrics tell you something is wrong, logs tell you why, and traces tell you where. Start with metrics for alerting, add logs for debugging, and add traces when latency across services is the primary concern.

items.question: What is the overhead of distributed tracing?
items.answer: Modern tracing systems with sampling add less than 1% CPU overhead. The real cost is storage and network egress for traces. Sample aggressively and store only what you need.

items.question: How do I prevent PII from appearing in logs and traces?
items.answer: Scrub PII at the instrumentation layer. Use log enrichment to redact sensitive fields before they leave the service. Add automated scanners to your CI pipeline that fail builds when new PII patterns are detected.

items.question: When should I use a dedicated observability vendor?
items.answer: When your team lacks the capacity to operate Prometheus, Grafana, and Jaeger reliably, or when correlation across logs, metrics, and traces is the primary bottleneck. Start with managed cloud tools and migrate to SaaS only when you need features they cannot provide.

data.title: Instrument the expense platform
data.description: Add structured logging, metrics, and distributed tracing to the expense API and background worker. Configure a Grafana dashboard showing the golden signals and a Jaeger trace for an expense submission.
steps: Add structured JSON logging to the API controllers and background worker
Define metrics for request count, latency, queue depth, and database connection pool usage
Instrument controllers and worker methods with OpenTelemetry spans
Create a Grafana dashboard with panels for each golden signal
Set an alert for error rate above 1% or p99 latency above 500ms
Verify the trace for an expense submission end to end in Jaeger
data.expectedOutcome: You should be able to explain how each signal helps during an incident and demonstrate the dashboard and trace in action.

data.title: Summary
points: Treat observability as a core feature, not an afterthought
Start with structured logs and golden-signal metrics before adding traces
Control costs with sampling, retention policies, and archiving
Build dashboards and alerts that your on-call team actually trusts
data.takeaway: Production is not a guessing game. The team that can answer 'what happened and why' in minutes instead of hours wins.
